Multislice CT (msCT) systems capture the energy-resolved X-ray attenuation at a single pixel to simultaneously enhance image quality, boost safety by lowering the delivered dose, and accelerate scans. Nevertheless, msCT data are inherently scarce and often corrupted by noise, posing significant reconstruction challenges. This study introduces a non-convex variational framework designed to reconstruct CT images, denois ct sensor noise, and perform quantitative material decomposition across a single CT scan. The approach utilizes an efficient proximal gradient algorithm supported by closed-form analytical expressions to calculate updates. Experimental evaluations were conducted on both simulated datasets and real-world msCT scans of a phantom, demonstrating the method's superior performance in reconstruction fidelity, denoising capabilities, and accuracy in material quantification compared to existing techniques.

Handwritten Text Recognition (HTR) is a vital area of research with significant real-world applications, particularly in developing nations where literacy rates are low. While deep learning has driven substantial recent advancements, it demands vast amounts of high-labeled training data, which is often unavailable for specific local handwriting styles or languages. To overcome this data scarcity, few-shot and zero-shot learning strategies have been explored; however, these methods often fail to deliver satisfactory performance in single-shot compositional HTR tasks involving both unfamiliar writing styles and new linguistic elements. This paper introduces a novel zero-shot data synthesis approach designed to enhance single-shot compositional HTR. By leveraging the inherent structure of language found in existing textual corpora, our method generates synthetic training samples that effectively bridge gaps between known and unknown scripts or languages. Experiments conducted on two datasets—one representing a new language and another introducing new handwriting—are performed using our technique alongside few-shot data augmentation. Results indicate that the proposed synthesis significantly boosts zero-shot single-shot compositional HTR performance, surpassing existing methods on both datasets.

This work introduces a novel approach to nuclear physics modeling by integrating the heavy nucleus computation capabilities of the Dirac-Hartree-Bogoliubov framework with the equation of state (EoS) analyses used in astrophysics. While previous DHBC models have been restricted to $Z \leq 110$, this study successfully extends the automatic, *ab initio* calculations up to lead ($^{208}\text{Pb}$). The study examines the properties of finite heavy nuclei and infinite nuclear matter, specifically the symmetry energy and its derivatives, alongside the analysis of field sources that drive matter within neutron stars.

The SSH model, a simple yet profound dimerized chain, serves as an accessible entryway for grasping key tenets of one-dimensional topological quantum mechanics. This paper offers a comprehensive analysis of the dual roles played by chiral and time-reversal symmetries within that framework. It begins by defining topological invariants for systems governed exclusively by chiral symmetry and proceeds to examine how these roles shift when both chiral and time-reversal symmetries are present. Furthermore, the study investigates the emergence of zero-energy states resulting from the breaking of these symmetries and concludes by mapping the model's phase diagram.

Recent research by Cima, Jimenez-Varella, and Zerbino investigates compact composition rules involving the Bergman spaces of bounded convex domains within $\mathbb{C}^n$. In contrast, this paper addresses analogous compact composition problems for mappings between two such convex domains and for compositions involving finite-dimensional spaces of polynomials restricted to specific convex sets. Additionally, we examine compact compositions arising from holomorphic maps defined on analytic disks situated in a bounded convex domain of $\mathbb{C}^n$.

We construct the dual-loop supergravity amplitude for N=4 super Yang-Mills theory on the AdS_5×S^5 background using its representation in terms of dual conformal cross-ratios. This supergravity result aligns precisely with the previously identified all-orders structure of the relevant part of the four-point function in the corresponding CFT.

Object-oriented programming (OOP) is widely adopted for high-level, expressive, and parallel software development, yet current general-purpose dynamic memory allocators (MLAs) for Graphics Processing Units (GPUs) struggle with the complex allocation patterns inherent in object-oriented designs. MLA performance is typically optimized for C-style procedural styles, resulting in inefficient memory utilization and excessive global memory reads when handling OOP workflows. Additionally, existing systems lack the flexibility to manage custom allocation policies required by specific object-oriented paradigms. To address these limitations, we introduce DynaSOAr, a novel, high-performance, customizable MLA engineered to support diverse object-oriented programming models on GPUs. DynaSOAr achieves this by integrating two core mechanisms: (1) a hybrid allocation strategy that combines global and local memory spaces to enhance both performance and memory efficiency, and (2) a multi-level free-list approach that accelerates the granular allocation of small memory blocks. Benchmark evaluations demonstrate that DynaSOAr delivers superior global memory access efficiency and customizable policy support compared to existing MLA solutions, resulting in an average 1.33× improvement in execution time and a 1.31× reduction in global memory read operations for object-oriented applications.

We examine the Stueckelberg mechanism within the standard $U(1)_X$ framework, analyzing its connection to the Stueckelberg mechanism in the parent $SO(10)$ theory. Our study focuses on how the $U(1)_X$ gauge boson acquires mass through Stueckelberg scalar fields, specifically investigating the influence of the $SO(10)$ breaking scale on the mass of this lightest boson. Furthermore, we explore the model's testability by outlining the potential signatures of this lightest boson at the LHC and future colliders, as well as its implications for the Higgs boson and the Stueckelberg fields themselves.

For a straw container subjected to internal pressure, the circumferential (hoop) stress is typically the dominant factor analyzed for integrity. This study examines the longitudinal stress instead, demonstrating that it remains significant even at low pressure levels. The research derives the relationship between stress and pressure, showing how longitudinal stress is influenced not only by pressure but also by the material's Poisson ratio and the ratio of straw length to diameter. The material properties were determined through a combination of literature review and experimental testing. These findings are visualized with representative graphs, and the proposed stress model is validated by comparing the results against established failure criteria.

The probabilistic object detection task involves identifying all instances of specific categories within an image while managing uncertainty regarding the number of detections per category. Although the Credal Bayesian Object Detection framework offers a principled approach to handling potential under-segments in visual tasks, its practical application is often hindered by the difficulty of precisely calculating the lower bound of the detection strength. This study introduces a streamlined Credal Bayesian framework that guarantees specific strength lower bounds, achievable through the constrained relaxation of probabilistic circuits. We propose several variations of Credal Bayesian networks, each supported by tailored constraint relaxations designed to accelerate the computation of strong guarantees. Empirical results demonstrate that our proposed methods outperform existing techniques, delivering both superior speed and certainty assurances.

We demonstrate that an accelerated frame induces a linear, space-dependent gauge potential within quantum mechanics. This finding suggests that an accelerating impurity in a superfluid bath generates the equivalent of an artificial Bloch crystal, opening a pathway to observe Bloch oscillations within superfluids and related quantum systems.

This paper demonstrates that the non-singularity table for generalised quadrangles can be structured into clusters, where each cluster corresponds to a specific neighbor-transitive code. We also establish that each cluster corresponds to a specific partial spread within the corresponding point graph. Furthermore, we provide general constructions of neighbor-transitive codes within these groups, utilizing codes derived from elliptic paraboloids and quadrics defined by equations of the type $x_0^2 + ax_1^2 + bx_1x_1 + cx_1^2 + dx_1 + ex_1 + f = 0$.

The Central Molecular Zone (CMZ) of the Milky Way represents a dense cluster of molecular gas and stars situated within a highly anisotropic environment. To investigate the spatial arrangement of the galaxy's central molecular molecular cloud complex, we analyzed archival data from the VLA's VLA Survey (VLAS) project, focusing on 1.3 mm continuum emission. We applied a novel technique calculating correlation functions within specific planes to assess how the positions of molecular clouds relate to one another. Our results reveal that the spatial configuration exhibits distinct anisotropy, showing a stronger tendency for clouds to align along the Galactic plane than in other directions. By modeling these observed correlation patterns with theoretical mass distributions, we determined that the observed anisotropy arises primarily from an elongated mass profile, where the major axis measures approximately 1.5 kpc and the minor axis spans roughly 0.3 kpc.

We introduce a non-linear high-fluence X-ray absorption model grounded in explicit electronic excitation rate equations. Our approach accounts for the dynamic evolution of bound-state electron populations across K-, L-, and M-shells, alongside continuum electrons, as they transition between various ionization stages. These rate equations, utilizing approximate transition probabilities, were integrated numerially with the absorption cross-section to simulate time-resolved spectra. When applied to synchrotron data from the platinum L-edges, our predictions for both spectral shape and absolute magnitude align closely with experimental observations. Notably, our simulation captures key high-fluence effects, including the dynamic depletion of inner-shell vacancies, Auger and fluorescence line-filling, and the consequent modification of absorption line profiles.

This study introduces a compact, energy-efficient, and wide-operating-voltage analog-to-digital temperature detection system. Utilizing a 0.18μm CMOS process, the sensor functions across a -40°C to 125°C range while powered between 0.6V and 1.8V. It achieves an exceptional energy efficiency of 1.06pJ per conversion and features a user-adjustable resolution ranging from 0.14°C to 0.24°C. The system operates at a conversion speed of 100ms, delivering superior accuracy with a maximum error of ±1.4°C and minimal area consumption of 0.011mm².

We introduce a heralded method for generating polarization entanglement between two photons that possess unequal intensities. By employing the "quantum scissors" formalism, we demonstrate that this approach functions as an efficient linear device for producing standard two-photon entangled states. Experiments utilizing type-II parametric down-conversion with beams containing approximately 100 photons on average confirm the generation of highly correlated polarization entangled pairs, where an average of roughly 0.87 emission events occur per quantum event.

Euclidean spanners serve as an efficient approximation for metric spaces, and their research has expanded significantly since the 1990s. This paper introduces and investigates a novel variant: the virtual Euclidean spanner. In this model, we maintain a base set of points in Euclidean space alongside an auxiliary spanner, allowing edges to exist between virtual connections formed by existing spanner paths. Specifically, we adapt the concept of the additive error, defining the spanner's quality by the maximum stretch across all edge estimates, where stretch measures the actual virtual distance relative to the estimated value. We present the construction of a $t$-dimensional spanner with $O(\epsilon^{-t} n^{1 + 4/t} \epsilon^{-t})$ edges that offers an $\epsilon$-approximation for any metric space, achieving a stretch of $e^\epsilon + 1$. We further examine specific scenarios, notably the two-dimensional case, to analyze the performance and properties of these structures.

Classifying IoT devices is essential for monitoring and managing smart homes and offices, especially as these devices become increasingly prevalent. While deep learning has proven effective for classification, it typically demands substantial electricity, memory, and processing power. To address this, we introduce a lightweight feature extraction method that enhances classification performance for edge IoT devices. By leveraging the low-cost, low-power capabilities of existing methods, this approach optimizes energy efficiency. Our solution utilizes a cost-aware strategy to select optimal features for a subsequent deep learning classifier. We evaluated our framework on two datasets, confirming that the framework improves device classification outcomes while minimizing energy consumption on resource-constrained IoT systems.

G\"odel modal logics, which rely on lattice-based semantics, have been extensively studied. This article introduces new algebraic and relational models for these logics and their extensions, with a specific focus on the interconnections among these various semantic frameworks.

This paper introduces a method for aligning words during translation, leveraging external bilingual knowledge bases such as Wikidata and BabelNet. By integrating this pre-existing bilingual data into our translation system, we achieve simultaneous word word alignment with no additional training data. This approach allows our model to perform word-level alignment on translated sentences in real time.

This work introduces a novel application of the distorted perturbation technique for generating Nash equilibria in finite games. Specifically, for a sufficiently large distortion parameter, the distorted expected utilities of all players serve as strict potential functions under the standard Euclidean probability metric. By leveraging this property, a gradient-based approach is developed to build a sequence that converges rapidly to a Nash equilibrium. Furthermore, using a gradient-free optimization strategy enables the generation of multiple equilibria, including the identification of previously unknown ones. Empirical results based on extensive numerical simulations demonstrate that this method outperforms current state-of-the-art algorithms in both efficiency and effectiveness.

We conducted an investigation into Primordial Black Hole (PBH) contributions to dark energy by performing cosmological simulations with PBESYCLE. This study introduces a novel library that integrates PBHs into the standard $\Lambda$CDM model, treating them as a component of dark energy. Within a $\Lambda$CDM+PBH framework, we examine the PBH mass function across a range of birth epochs and densities, simulating their subsequent evolution. We assess the viability of this model by comparing predictions against current observational datasets, specifically Type Ia Supernovae (SN Ia) luminosity distances and Baryon Acoustic Oscillations (BAO) measurements. Our analysis reveals that a PBH population capable of constituting dark energy must be extremely monochromatic, confined to a narrow mass window of approximately one order of magnitude. Furthermore, the initial mass function's narrowness must tighten as the PBH mass increases.

This study examines the interaction of two rigid, tapered objects, such as pyramids, where their contact is mediated by a granular collection of spheres. The configuration is defined by the distance between the objects and their mutual rotation angle. The potential energy surface features multiple local minima, indicating stable states at various contact angles and separations. The research focuses on the system's transition dynamics between these equilibria, specifically analyzing how the granular material's properties—such as grain size and count—influence the transition time. The observed temporal evolution exhibits three distinct phases: an initial rapid shift in angle, a secondary slower adjustment in separation distance, and a final stage of minor corrections in both angle and gap. The initial rapid phase is interpreted as the objects effectively acting as a single unit before the granular medium allows individual object dynamics to emerge in subsequent stages.

This work examines a class of spherical static random fields that are fully specified by their Gaussian nature and the first two coefficients of their spectral representation. The primary objective is to develop one-step ahead prediction auto-recurrence equations for both the fields themselves and their gradients. Additionally, we derive corresponding spatial auto-recurrence relations. The selection of specific field types ensures that prediction challenges are effectively transformed into problems of optimal linear estimation within a structured triangular array of Gaussian random variables.

The quantum Szegedy–Beniova–Vazirani (QSBV) protocol enables the reconstruction of an unknown pure quantum state's density matrix by performing repeated projections onto arbitrary basis states. However, this method's efficiency relies on the assumption of high engagement rates between particles and detectors, a condition that is frequently difficult to satisfy in practical scenarios such as quantum imaging with single photons. This study introduces a novel reconstruction algorithm that bypasses the need for calculating engagement rates and functions effectively even when engagement is zero. The new method leverages quantum phase estimation, utilizing only a minimal number of detected particles to achieve state reconstruction. Experimental validation was conducted through quantum tomography of a qubit state prepared within a standard superconducting circuit, demonstrating successful state characterization. The proposed approach opens new possibilities for quantum tasks using undetected particles, including enhanced quantum sensing and the development of more efficient quantum algorithms.

The study of frictional forces between liquid foams and solid surfaces has garnered significant attention in recent years due to the critical role these forces play in diverse applications, ranging from enhanced oil recovery to food technology and fire suppression. This research introduces a novel experimental method to measure the shear stress experienced by wall-adjacent liquid foams. By employing a rotating cylinder setup, we successfully replicated the characteristic 'wall texture' formed by coalesced bubbles in various confined foam systems. Our measurements reveal that frictional stress scales with the applied shear rate in a manner consistent with Bingham plastic fluid behavior, demonstrating that apparent yield stress results from the mechanical resistance of the wall-adjacent foam structure. Furthermore, we examined how foam properties—including bubble size distribution, surface chemistry, and bulk concentration—influence this rheological response. The observed mechanics are explained by a mechanical model that accounts for both the coalescence of bubbles at the wall and the subsequent rearrangement of the coarsening foam texture.

The identification of skin cancer is critical for effective treatment and improved patient survival. While dermatologists typically diagnose the condition by examining moles through visual inspection and microscopy, this traditional approach is often constrained by the inspector's limited experience and subjective variability. In contrast, this paper introduces a deep learning framework designed to classify skin lesions and detect malignancy. Initially, a ResNet model is employed to extract features from image samples, which are subsequently fed into a two-stage classification system. This system utilizes a Softmax layer for final lesion categorization and applies the Entropy metric to identify and filter out outlier data points that deviate significantly from standard patterns.

We report on a time- and angle-resolved photoemission study of sodium, a prototypical metallic system. Our results indicate that the photoemission signals align with a semi-Heisenberg model featuring an almost-free electron model. The measured quasi-particle lifetimes are consistent with prior angle-resolved photoemission findings, yet they exceed expectations for a Fermi liquid theory. Furthermore, time-of-flight neutron scattering data support these quasi-particle lifetime observations.

This paper presents a new approach to analyze area variation in dynamical systems, characterized by its simplicity, accessibility, and broad applicability. The proposed method relies on computing specific path integrals along curves, such as Hamiltonian paths, within phase space. The authors demonstrate the procedure through examples in both one and two degrees of freedom, with detailed application to the free expansion of an ideal gas.

We calculate the Kovalevich weights for specific curving and link graphs that appear in deformation quantizations of symplectic manifolds featuring non-trivial underlying Poisson structures. In this work, we demonstrate a method for determining these weights by utilizing an associated algebraic curvature structure. As a result, we establish a technique that enables the derivation of the weights for curving and link graphs involving any number of inversions and cables.

This study examines non-linear traveling waves within one-dimensional non-symmetric periodic lattices, focusing on the stability of localized, non-dynamically rescaled, non-oscillatory nanoptera. The analysis proceeds in two phases: first, the problem is treated analytically for a non-symmetric woodpile arrangement, and secondly, it is addressed numerically for a diatomic chain featuring a non-symmetric mass configuration. The initial phase involves an asymptotic analysis of the non-linear woodpile system regarding non-oscillatory nanoptera, deriving the non-trivial mass-transport scaling law for amplitudes as $\varepsilon^{1/2}$, where $\varepsilon$ represents the small non-linearity parameter. The subsequent phase utilizes a non-variational, non-self-adjoint spectral problem to investigate the stability of these states, employing a non-traditional, non-variational approach to the spectral problem. The stability analysis reveals a non-variational, non-variational spectral problem, revealing a non-variational, non-variational mass-transport scaling law for amplitudes as $\varepsilon^{1/2}$, where $\varepsilon$ represents the small non-linearity parameter, where the non-variational, non-variational mass-transport scaling law for amplitudes as $\varepsilon^{1/2}$, where the non-variational, non-variational mass-transport

The detection of primordial non-Gaussianity serves as a crucial avenue for investigating the early universe and its fundamental underpinnings. While cosmological collider physics offers a promising framework for uncovering high-energy physics residing at scales far beyond direct experimental reach, the traditional approach has faced challenges due to difficulties in precisely defining and extracting correlation functions arising from particle exchanges between interaction instances. This paper proposes a resolution to that problem, demonstrating how to effectively extract such signals using worldlines and light rays. Furthermore, we identify and analyze "primal features"—distinct imprints of exchange particles that appear within correlation spectra under the high-contrast limit. These primal features offer an alternative method for characterizing cosmological collider signals and are expected to facilitate more efficient computational techniques for extracting exchange correlation functions in the future.

This paper introduces a new family of graphs known as "accordion charts," defined by a specific geometric arrangement of points and lines. We establish a one-to-one correspondence between these graphs and a specific category of circ graphs, denoted as $C(3a, b)$. Our results demonstrate that within this family, every bridge and every perfect matching can be explicitly defined. Furthermore, the text provides an identification of isomorphism classes for all graphs in this family of size $n \leq 100$. As a concluding application, we prove that each accordion chart graph is also a connected quarters circulant graph.

We investigate the quantum-mechanical dynamics of a single particle constrained to a one-dimensional lattice with finite sites, allowing movement only between adjacent states. The system's evolution is driven by a Hamiltonian that incorporates a localized three-phase state within the energy spectrum, which induces a corresponding shift in a particle's quantum walk. By examining this model across various parameters, we demonstrate that the dynamics exhibit dynamical scaling behavior, where the characteristic timescales and spatial extension of the evolution expand significantly when the energy approaches an embedded resonance. Furthermore, we find that the dynamical timescales are governed by the localization times associated with a quasi-stationary state, a concept that proves instrumental in elucidating the general principles of the walk's behavior.

Self-distillation has emerged as a prominent research area in deep learning, enabling models to maintain high performance even when trained on limited data or computational resources. Although current self-distillation methods for Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) have achieved significant success, they often struggle with Self-Attention models like Vision Transformers (ViT). This paper introduces a self-distillation framework tailored for ViTs, guided by an alignment between the Self-Attention mechanisms and the Weighted Summation processes inherent to CNN upsampling/downsampling operations. Our method employs an innovative cross-image loss function that enforces consistency in both teacher and student ViTs regarding their internal self-attention weights. Empirical results demonstrate that this approach yields substantial improvements in various object detection and segmentation tasks, specifically enhancing performance by 2.4% and 1.6%, respectively, on the COCO dataset.

We introduce a dissipative dark fluid model incorporating both dark matter and dark energy components. By incorporating the bulk viscosity coefficient into the dark fluid's equation of state, we explore a scenario where energy dissipation occurs within the dark sector. Our analysis examines the system's dynamical behavior through a detailed DSA (Stability and Dynamical Systems Analysis) of the non-linear ordinary differential equations governing the model's parameters. We demonstrate that our model naturally reproduces a $\Lambda$CDM-like universe by identifying stable attractor solutions that correspond to an accelerating expansion phase. Furthermore, we assess the model's viability using current cosmological datasets, specifically the Type Ia Supernovae (Pantheon) catalog, baryon acoustic oscillation (BAO) measurements, and Hubble parameter ($H(z)$) data. Our findings indicate that the model offers a fitting quality comparable to the standard $\Lambda$CDM framework. Additionally, we derive and analyze the statefinder $z$-source parameter to investigate the evolutionary history of the universe under this new dissipative dark fluid model.

We provide a direct demonstration of the ill-posedness of the neutral Euler equations in critical Sobolev spaces. By utilizing finite-dimensional nilpotent Lie groups, we construct a sequence of regular initial conditions converging to zero in the relevant norm, for which arbitrarily small remainders generate global strong solutions that diverge significantly in size.

Although recent advancements in image generation models have achieved remarkable realism, they frequently overlook meaningful content. We introduce the Steady Creator, an approach that integrates conditional steady-state distributions into the diffusion process within latent realms to enhance both conditional adherence and steady-state consistency. By utilizing a conditional steady-state consistency module, diffusion steps are directed toward semantically stable regions of the latent space corresponding to specific topics, thereby reinforcing conditional retention. Additionally, a new Steady Creator Image Realm (CRI-Realm) is constructed in lower-dimensional latent space to facilitate more precise guidance. Within this CRI-Realm, conditional steady-state consistency is further enhanced by leveraging conditional image embeddings derived from a pre-trained vision encoder. Empirical results demonstrate that the Steady Creator outperforms existing methods in both conditional adherence and steady-state consistency, with applications extending to image editing and the generation of diagnostic medical images.

This paper introduces a new method for Bayesian neural networks designed to enable reversible data concealment. By defining a specific Bayesian neural network for image reconstruction, we develop an efficient variational inference procedure for training the encoder. This encoder subsequently hides data within carrier images, while a dedicated decoder, utilizing the inferred posterior samples, successfully retrieves the embedded information. Experimental outcomes confirm that our approach achieves superior embedding capacities and post-extraction image quality compared to existing techniques.

This study investigates the potential significance of $J/\psi$ decays into photons plus invisible particles. We demonstrate that such a process could constrain low-energy Effective Field Theories (EFTs) describing neutrino mass generation and primordial dark energy production. Specifically, we establish a link between the decay width $\Gamma(J/\psi\to \gamma+\text{invisible})$ and the primordial energy density of dark energy, noting that current experimental upper limits on $\Gamma(J/\psi\to \gamma+\text{invisible})$ already yield significant bounds on the universe's initial energy scale. We further explore how improved measurements of this decay mode could inform LHC analyses of Higgs self-coupling.

Magnetic bright spots (MBS) are small, short-lived solar features that exhibit stronger magnetic flux and higher temperatures than photospheric elements. While their exact nature remains debated, this study provides observational evidence supporting a two-part distribution for MBS properties, including size, lifetime, magnetic flux, and temperature. Specifically, we analyzed the size-duration relationship for MBS observed on the solar disk, utilizing size estimates derived from filtergram intensity profiles and duration measurements from temporal intensity variations. The observed distribution is well-modeled as a bimodal mixture of a lognormal and a power-law function. This finding suggests two distinct populations of MBS: one with durations under 2 days, characterized by smaller sizes, and another with durations exceeding 2 days, which are larger. These larger, longer-lived spots are linked to the lifespans of magnetic flux tubes, whereas the shorter-lived, smaller spots are governed by granular timescales.

Current one-shot identification models for action recognition rely on hand-crafted clips whose fixed duration ignores the inherent temporal variability of real-world gesture timing. This study investigates whether natural "minimal clips"—short, essential action segments—can serve as a superior alternative to traditional predefined segments. Findings indicate that action minima are not only easy to detect automatically but also highly effective for identification. Furthermore, we present a novel network architecture capable of learning action clips by harnessing human-provided minimal videos. Ultimately, this research demonstrates that leveraging human-defined minimal clips can match or exceed the performance of standard pre-set clip methods in recognizing motor activities.

Observations indicate that galaxy-wide magnetic fields endure for hundreds of millions of years, defying standard models that fail to explain the sufficient strength of these fields. We propose that a shadow form of the dark matter sector, interacting via a gauge symmetry $U(1)'$ with the standard model through "milli-magnetic monopole" coupling, offers a solution. This framework allows our Galaxy's initial post-recombination magnetic field to be preserved by this monopole shadow matter, given its extremely low but non-zero interaction cross-section with ordinary matter, which enables effective energy transfer to the visible sector. We further demonstrate that energy dissipation caused by monopole-induced Bremsstrahlung radiation is counterbalanced by a reaction force opposing Galactic rotation, thereby preventing Galactic wind and ensuring the stability of the galaxy's structure.

Accurately predicting future spatiotemporal patterns of climate variables is vital for assessing risks related to global climate change. Traditional methods often fail to capture complex, nonlinear relationships within these variables, while existing deep learning models struggle with long-term dependencies and cross-domain interactions in climate data. This study introduces STFormer, a novel self-supervised transformer model designed specifically for predicting spatio-temporal climate datasets. The architecture utilizes two key mechanisms: patchified 2D inputs processed through a shifted window-based Cross-Attention module to handle long-range dependencies, and a channel-wise Self-Attention layer to model inter-channel correlations. Empirical results using synthetic data alongside real-world examples for rainfall and sea surface temperature confirm that STFormer surpasses current benchmarks in predicting both tasks.

We examine a two-component dark matter scenario within a Complex Scalar Extension of the Standard Model featuring Higgs doublets, specifically $S_3$-symmetric models with CP conservation. In this setup, dark matter candidates are identified as the complex components of one scalar triplet. We analyze the phenomenology of these candidates through the lens of both direct and indirect detection methods, as well as collider experiments. The study demonstrates that the phenomenology of these DM candidates closely resembles that of the real triplet scalar Dark Matter previously explored in the literature.

We define the PPT quadrilateral hypothesis (PPTH) as the assertion that any entropy inequality valid for all PPT states on a quadrilateral of quantum states is also valid generally. We demonstrate that the PPTH is logically equivalent to the long-standing distillation conjecture. Furthermore, we illustrate the relevance of PPTH by examining four specific scenarios involving entropic relations: the entanglement cost, distillable key, single-shot distillation rate, and single-copy entanglement—each governed by corresponding relations between entanglement measures. Our analysis reveals that PPTH holds universally for the entanglement cost and distillable key (both defined for infinite copies), as well as for both the single-shot and single-copy scenarios regarding the distillable key. We introduce a PDE-constrained optimization framework to model glial regulation of neuronal cytosolic substance transport and congestion, a process vital for brain function. In this system, a C-shaped neuron and an adjacent star-shaped glial cell share an interface that facilitates exchange fluxes. The glia regulates incoming ionic fluxes to a neuron, aiming to maintain homeostasis by optimizing a cost functional that penalizes deviations from homeostatic levels, flux magnitude, and concentration gradients. The convection-diffusion equations governing neuronal substance transport are subject to this cost functional, which serves as the objective to be minimized through gradient-based methods. Gradient computations rely on an adjoint approach to account for congestion effects within the neuron. The proposed methodology is validated using a simplified 2D geometry, and its efficacy is demonstrated with realistic parameters for a neuron and glial cell of approximate dimensions $10 \mu m \times 10 \mu m$.

Fraud detection in digital banking is a critical challenge, and our study introduces a new approach to identifying money laundering schemes by leveraging network motifs. We analyzed the largest available transaction dataset, comprising 1.2 billion transfers among 11.5 million users, and applied motif-based analysis to the resulting financial network. Our findings reveal that tripartite motifs are significantly more prevalent than other structures, suggesting they are essential for understanding transaction patterns. Notably, we discovered a strong correlation between tripartite motifs and specific fraud patterns, leading to the creation of NeMo, a fraud detection system that utilizes this network structure. NeMo achieved a high F1-score of 0.893 on a money laundering detection task, demonstrating its effectiveness.

We examine the electromagnetic emissions generated as a white dwarf spirals into a black hole, utilizing a self-consistent radiative transfer code to model a fully stratified system. This code accounts for the absorption and emission of photons, relativistic beaming, Doppler shifts, scattering, as well as absorption and emission mechanisms from atoms, ions, and molecules. Our simulations span optical, infrared, and radio frequencies, covering radii from the accreting body's surface up to approximately 100 radii. As the white dwarf is compressed by the black hole, tidal disruption triggers intense accretion and heating of the surrounding gas cloud. Consequently, the gas emits powerful radiation across optical, infrared, and radio spectra. Our findings indicate that the observed spectrum is heavily shaped by the white dwarf's own internal thermal structure, the specific accretion dynamics, and the physical conditions of the circumstellar environment.

We examine the form factors arising from light baryon transitions within semileepy $\tau$-decays involving three bodies, employing a quark-based model. The analysis covers the complete set of relevant form factors, including those associated with the lightest baryons ($N$ and $\Delta$), and constructs the corresponding hadronic current. Additionally, we address the calculation of $\tau$-decay branching ratios for transitions to nucleons and the $\Delta$ baryons.

The study introduces a family of Tversky metrics parameterized by $\alpha \in [1, \infty)$, beginning with the established Jaccard distance at $\alpha=1$ and extending towards the normalized information distance at the limit $\alpha \to \infty$.

Deblurring degrades image quality, causing downstream tasks to suffer. While existing solutions often focus on specific scenarios, this work introduces a unified approach to deblur both images and video for human and scene motion. This challenge is modeled as a conditional generation task using pseudo-blur pairs, where a generator creates blur pairs for training deblur networks. These networks are trained on public datasets but applied to private videos via pseudo-blur synthesis, demonstrating state-of-the-art results on both training and unseen data. The proposed methodology offers the first general deblur benchmark for motion in images and video, complete with thorough comparisons.

Although framework-supported language extensions have demonstrated the feasibility of molecular-scale computation, designing new programs for these digital molecular devices remains arduous due to the stochastic nature of DNA-based communication, DNA affinity, and hybridization. To address this, the study introduces a specific design for a stochastic Spiking Leaky Integrate-and-fire (SLIF) neuron utilizing a strand-displacement circuit framework. This research marks the inaugural demonstration of a SLIF neuron fully realized through DNA strand-displacement circuits, with its oscillatory and spiking dynamics successfully simulated using two distinct programming frameworks, Mozart and p5DNA.

The ultrapower associated with this sequence, denoted $I(\mathbb{N})/\mathcal{U}$, is formed by taking the quotient of the space of all such sequences over an ultrafilter $\mathcal{U}$ on $\mathbb{N}$. This quotient space is equipped with a natural partial order derived from the original poset. A fundamental result establishes that this structure forms a linearly ordered set (completeness aside) precisely when the poset $A$ possesses a specific property: being co-finitely bounded. This condition means that for any upper bound set $I$ (an element greater than or equal to all members of the set), the complement of $I$ within $A$ is finite.

The completeness of the resulting ordered group $I(\mathbb{N})/\mathcal{U}$ is then investigated under the assumption that the underlying poset $A$ satisfies the co-finite bounded condition. Data profiling is a well-established technique for examining the internal structure of datasets to identify anomalies and define data characteristics. Although current tools are versatile enough to profile various data streams, they lack the ability to account for specific dataset profiles. This paper introduces the concept of dataset-particular profiling and outlines a methodology for its implementation. The proposed method was tested using the BDDDataset, a collection of real-world datasets drawn from data competitions. The findings demonstrate that dataset profiles contain distinct and discernible traits, underscoring the necessity of adopting this approach.

Recent research has highlighted the significant potential of correntropy as a robust metric for nonlinear system analysis and signal processing, particularly due to its ability to utilize only a localized segment of data. However, the correntropy criterion offers no inherent guidance regarding the selection of its kernel bandwidth. To address this gap, the current study proposes a new graph-based signal estimation framework. By integrating generalized correntropy with graph Laplacian regularizers, the method ensures sturdiness while effectively capturing both local and global data structures. Furthermore, the paper introduces a kernel adaptation strategy that jointly optimizes bandwidth selection and signal recovery. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed algorithm outperforms existing methods, delivering superior recovery accuracy even under noisy conditions and non-Gaussian environments.

We describe the creation of custom-designed, highly robust quantum states using an entangled spinor interferometer. These states are tailored to optimize specific measurement outcomes, allowing for precision frequency estimation that exceeds the standard quantum limit and is even immune to photon loss. The observed superiority in both measurement accuracy and resilience is validated through comparisons with conventional squeezed states. The entire framework for generating these states is entirely optical and easily scalable.

The initial Robin eigenvalue associated with a given bounded open subset $\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^n$ and the nonlinear elliptic operator $A(u) = \text{div}(|\nabla u|^{p-2}\nabla u) - \lambda_1(\Omega,R)$ is estimated with high accuracy. Specifically, we establish precise upper and lower bounds for $\lambda_1(\Omega,R)$ derived from the precise positive solution $u$ of the corresponding Dirichlet problem within $\Omega$. Furthermore, we prove that as the Robin boundary parameter $R$ approaches infinity, this eigenvalue converges to the precise Dirichlet eigenvalue of $A(u)$.

Recent advancements in deep learning have yielded significant breakthroughs in graph-structured data analysis, a success largely attributed to Graph Convolutional Neural Networks (GCN). Despite their widespread adoption, the theoretical underpinnings of GCN remain elusive. This study introduces a novel approach to comprehending graph convolution by examining matched filtering—a technique that has historically provided clear theoretical validation for convolution in both image and audio processing. By applying this method to graphs, we gain enhanced theoretical clarity regarding the semantics of GCN operations, thereby revealing both their strengths and limitations. Ultimately, this work not only demystifies the reasoning behind why GCN achieves remarkable efficacy in semantically segmented tasks, such as node classification and graph classification, but also offers practical, empirically supported suggestions for addressing its specific weaknesses.

Contextualized automatic training (CA) represents a significant advancement in automatic language modeling, enabling models to perform well even with limited, specialized domain data. However, CA systems demand substantial computational resources for both training and inference, which hinders their practical application. This study proposes a solution by integrating CA with pre-trained language models (PLMs), creating a new framework called deep contextualized auto-training (CAp). The goal is to reduce CA requirements for large volumes of contextualized training sets by leveraging PLMs' extensive existing knowledge. Evaluations conducted across three diverse domains—finance, health, and law—demonstrate that CAp surpasses traditional self-trained methods and delivers even greater improvements over pre-trained baselines. Furthermore, these results highlight the model's robustness and flexibility across varying training data scenarios.

The semi-inclusive decay $B\to D\ell\nu_\ell$ has been examined using a light-front quark framework to determine transition form factors without invoking model-dependent assumptions. In this study, wave functions for the $B$ and $D$ mesons are derived by enforcing consistency with their respective sum rules for squared masses. The form factors $f_+(q^2)$ and $f_0(q^2)$ are computed directly from light-front quark wave functions, while the scalar form factor $f_\mathcal{S}(q^2)$ emerges as a linear combination of light-front quark-quark correlation and light-front meson light-cone distribution amplitudes. Light-front quark framework predictions for light-form factors align well with experimental data and previous phenomenological analyses. Furthermore, the branching ratio for $B\to D^{\ast*}\ell\nu_\ell$ is calculated, yielding a value of $(10.3\pm 0.4)\%$, which agrees satisfactorily with experimental measurements.

In the context of the pi-calculus, we define and examine a form of non-reversible, symmetric reduction that permits transitions independent of direction. To analyze this reduction in relation to reversible, symmetric pi-calculus concepts—specifically the brims—we introduce the notion of membrane-based brims. These membranes, capable of both nesting and movement, enable the controlled, symmetric propagation of brims. Furthermore, we demonstrate the controlled, symmetric decrease of distance between processes through the strategic use of membranes, all within a setting of non-reversible, symmetric computation.

The original Cai, \u00dcmmerman, and Immerman (CFI) construction achieves a reduction from the symmetric group to the graph isomorphism problem within polynomial time, yet this efficiency relies on generating a specific collection of abelian subgroups. This paper introduces a new, unrestricted CFI construction that operates in polynomial time under the assumption that the network used to build the resulting graphs possesses high symmetry. The paper also details a method for expanding graphs into larger examples while maintaining or enhancing their overall symmetry. Finally, the authors present graph families that achieve full polynomial generation for both the input graphs and their corresponding CFI reduction instances, all without depending on the generation of any预先 defined abelian groups.

The substitution of bismuth in Eu2Ir2O7—a material characterized by strong electron-electron correlations and a ground state involving a gap due to Mott physics—was examined via Bi doping. Hard X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (HAXPES) data revealed a progressive reduction in the energy gap as Bi concentration increased, culminating in the disappearance of the gap at a x=0.25 doping level. This transition point aligns with findings from other experimental techniques. Furthermore, the valence band spectra for samples with x≥0.25 displayed significant similarities to those of the metallic compound Sr2Ir2O7. These observations indicate that the insulating-to-metal phase shift in this series results from the weakening of inter-site interactions caused by Bi substitution, rather than the activation of electronic correlations.

This article investigates the properties of finite-dimensional set-valued mappings, with a specific focus on those in two dimensions. It establishes new criteria for the existence of single-valued Lipschitz selections for these mappings and introduces two distinct methods for characterizing the graph of a 2-Dimensional Set-Valued Mapping (2D-SVM) as the boundary of a convex set. Additionally, the work outlines two approaches for constructing these mappings: either by approximating the graph of the 2D-SVM using finite unions of polytopes or by generating selections through the convexification of the graph's boundary. These developments are supported by multiple examples and applications, including new solvability conditions for constrained optimization problems and the creation of multi-valued convex programs.

Probability assignments for events that cannot be linearly ordered present a significant challenge. In this paper, we examine a scenario involving three such events, $A$, $B$, and $C$, where a circular relationship exists: $A$ is more likely than $C$, $C$ is more likely than $B$, yet $A$ is more likely than $B$. While circular preferences are typically associated with irrationality, we argue that these probabilities can possess both magnitude and relative likelihood, thereby enabling consistency across the three comparisons. Consequently, certain properties of nontransitivity may actually illuminate our understanding of circularity in probability theory.

In the run-time environment, dynamic object linking and memory allocation are essential for allocating and initializing the extensive number of software components that make up modern systems. Conversely, during compile time, a smaller set of components is handled, where object linking and memory reservation occur proactively to streamline the execution process. This paper presents a novel concept called the Run-time Setup Space (RSS), a dedicated memory area used to store the auxiliary data structures and auxiliary code fragments required to support runtime dynamic linking and memory management. We further introduce a specialized compiler analysis technique designed to shift the preparation of this RSS content from the run-time phase to compile time. By moving these activities earlier, the system aims to diminish the overhead associated with runtime setup procedures, resulting in faster program execution.

Direct detection experiments for light dark matter (DM) typically investigate the production of nuclear recoil, whereas heavy DM candidates are usually sought through nuclear recoil at high energies, and sub-GeV to GeV-scale DM through nuclear recoil at low energies. For the intermediate mass range, however, the nuclear recoil energy becomes so significant that it can induce full nuclear disintegration. In this study, we demonstrate that this process generates ionization signals resembling those from atomic electron recoil, thereby becoming the primary channel for detecting intermediate-mass DM. We analyze the phenomenology of this novel interaction and calculate the corresponding spin-independent and spin-dependent cross-sections for direct detection. Furthermore, by incorporating recent data from SENSEI and other relevant experiments, we derive constraints on the spin-independent and spin-dependent cross-sections for intermediate-mass DM.

We introduce an anti-Jaynes-Cummings model featuring a multi-level atom coupled to an input single-photon wavepacket aimed at generating nonclassical optical pulse trains. Our analysis reveals that both energy transfer efficiency and the rates of excitation and entanglement generation rely critically on the photon wavepacket's temporal shape, with Rabi oscillations inverted compared to the standard Jaynes-Cummings framework. We examine how varying atomic levels influence transmission properties and entanglement generation, noting that an anti-Raman-Nath coupling regime yields higher entanglement than a Carrer-Pennington-like coupling regime. Furthermore, we investigate the generation of superpositions of Fock states within the atomic system, observing that optimal generation of anti-Rabi oscillcations, excitation, and entanglement occurs when the input is a Fock state rather than a wavepacket. We demonstrate the creation of distinct nonclassical states, including anti-squeezed and anti-super-Radiant squeezed single photons, as well as superpositions thereof. Finally, we confirm that optimized conditions for energy transfer, excitation probability, and entanglement generation coincide when the input consists of a Fock state.

This study introduces a distinct method for estimating Inter-Beat Intervals (IBIs) using the Tiramisu model, characterized by its ability to accurately filter out noise and the respiratory signal from raw ECG data while assessing irregular heart rhythms. By applying downsampling to raw ECG signals, the model achieves precise QRS detection with minimal error. Furthermore, the proposed approach demonstrates superior accuracy in detecting IBIs when compared to conventional methods.

Active matter encompasses self-propelled entities that consume internal energy for movement, a field that has recently attracted significant scientific interest. This study investigates the collective behavior of an active particle model governed by an internal energy consumption mechanism linked to labor, which follows an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process. We analyze how activity levels, propulsive force fluctuations, and labor correlate with one another, examining their impact on mean-squared displacement and the emergence of phase transitions in both individual and group dynamics. By examining how velocity correlations, energy consumption, and activity interconnect, we determine that labor variations serve as a robust indicator of particle state, enabling precise activity classification. Furthermore, we identify a correlation between labor fluctuations and the intensity of the phase transition characterizing active motion.

Introducing HUMBI is a comprehensive dataset featuring 30,000 human body gestures captured via 12 synchronized motion capture (MoCap) systems, designed to model diverse natural movements. Gesture recognition remains a difficult task in computer vision and computer graphics, particularly for modeling the variability inherent in natural human movement. To address this, we developed a benchmark challenge and evaluation protocol, dividing the dataset into a training set of 10,000 gestures from 8 motion capture systems and a test set of 20,000 gestures from the remaining 4. The provided training data includes 3D gesture categories, 3D gesture instances, and associated gesture labels. The study evaluates 3D instance segmentation, gesture detection, and 3D gesture classification methods, with a specific focus on gesture classification. We present baseline results derived from two distinct approaches: (1) extracting local features from point clouds to classify them using off-the-shelf classifiers, and (2) training a deep neural network on point cloud instance segments for classification.

Although cross-lingual transfer learning for speech recognition is well-established, existing literature largely ignores the critical challenge of aligning speech features across languages. Current solutions either fail to scale effectively or demand extensive retraining when languages are introduced. This paper presents a neural task representation method for speech recognition that facilitates model-agnostic multilingual transfer without requiring additional data or specific retraining. By leveraging language-universal task representations, the approach enhances the alignment of speech features regardless of language. Empirical results demonstrate that this method achieves substantial performance gains in speech recognition, specifically for lesser-studied languages.

This paper introduces a straightforward yet highly effective approach for video super-resolution, building upon the foundational BasicVSR model. We address two primary deficiencies in existing enhancement-based Video SR methods: the insufficient propagation and misalignment of features across scales. To remedy these issues, we employ a comprehensive strategy that integrates spatial and temporal alignment with the careful propagation of features. Specifically, we utilize an improved propagation mechanism that facilitates the deep storage of spatial details in an internal feature buffer, ensuring these features remain stable and uniform throughout the video sequence. Furthermore, we implement a multi-level alignment process to sharpen the precise registration of spatial and temporal features, while a novel high-performance decoder effectively restores the final high-resolution output. Extensive testing confirms that BasicVSR++ surpasses current state-of-the-art results in both high and very high computational efficiency scenarios.

We introduce a modular approach to reinforcement learning (RL) designed to accelerate the convergence of shared policies across multiple interfaces. Our method employs model-based RL to construct task-specific dynamics for each task, which enables the rapid convergence of separate task policies. These learned task policies then inform a shared prior, guiding the exploration of the modular system. We evaluate this framework in a multi-agent version of the multi-agent cart-pole task, demonstrating its ability to master all subtasks and successfully identify an optimal configuration for the combined system.

We introduce a finite-duration thermal engine operating between two heat baths at distinct temperatures, where the system's evolution is restricted to an ideal, uniparametric dilational control protocol. The study analyzes both the average work output and power generation across various restricted dynamical frameworks, including classical and quantum scenarios. By employing an approximate, long-lasting heat engine model, power generation is maximized using optimal dilation protocols. Furthermore, power is found to depend on the system's characteristic time scales, specifically the duration of the evolution and the heat bath correlation time. In contrast, power output remains independent of the system's intrinsic dynamics. Finally, it is demonstrated that finite, ideal dilational engines can achieve zero net entropy production, thereby satisfying the conditions for reversibility.

Hurricanes represent one of the most severe natural disasters, capable of inflicting catastrophic damage on the United States through high-speed winds, heavy rainfall, and storm surges. Although the frequency and intensity of these storms are projected to rise as a result of climate change, the specific impacts of surge, wind, and rain on the national power grid remain poorly understood. This study introduces a spatiotemporal model designed to evaluate the resilience of energy infrastructure against varying surge levels, wind speeds, and precipitation. The research utilizes surge, wind, and rain data from the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) alongside historical vegetation and infrastructure failure records from the United States Energy Information Administration (EIA). Findings indicate that while storm and rain frequencies significantly influence vegetation failure rates, surge events have negligible effects. Furthermore, the analysis reveals distinct spatial and temporal patterns in vegetation outages, with similar observations made regarding storm damage to infrastructure. The authors conclude by suggesting directions for future research.

This result serves as a unique continuation theorem for these eigenfunctions and is also applicable to monogenic functions using three-spheres valuated in the complex plane using the maximum principle for harmonic functions.

We investigate the prospects for detecting new physics involving extended scalar sectors at the LHC and the High-Luminosity phase, focusing on scenarios where additional neutral scalar states appear alongside a non-trivial network of couages. By analyzing vacuum stability requirements and flavor constraints, we establish the theoretical boundaries for these models. We then detail the methodology for analyzing scalar sector vacuum decay chains and identify the optimal production and decay channels to probe these scenarios. Finally, we demonstrate the utility of machine learning techniques in disentangling overlapping scalar signatures and enhance the sensitivity of existing analyses.

This study introduces Quasi-Periodic WaveNet (QPNet), an autoregressive model designed for raw waveform synthesis that integrates pitch control via dilated convolution. While WaveNet and its accelerated variant, WaveGLow, have demonstrated significant advancements in speech and music generation, their inherent stochastic nature results in inconsistent pitch and timbre, limiting their utility for music creation. Although prior attempts to implement pitch-guided synthesis rely on conditioning the input on pitch information, these methods often fail to produce synthetically accurate audio due to WaveNet's inductive bias toward predicting only one-step ahead samples. To overcome this limitation, we propose QPNet, which employs a set of shared convolutions with dilation factors that are powers of two. This specific architecture enables the network to learn long-term dependencies with a reduced number of layers, allowing it to generate two samples per time step while effectively modeling quasi-periodic waveforms. Our model was trained on the NSFC-2.4m dataset to synthesize Chinese monophonic speech. Listening tests indicate that QPNet generates audio of superior perceptual quality and higher pitch fidelity compared to standard WaveNet and WaveGLow models.

Traditional collaborative filtering (CF) methods often struggle with noisy, sparse, and incomplete user preference data, which can result in inaccurate recommendations. To overcome these limitations, this paper introduces a novel bi-cluster-based CF approach tailored to the specific local bi-clusters within a user's profile. This system facilitates interactions between users sharing similar tastes by leveraging those similarity signals, utilizing a hybrid fusion of content-based and CF techniques to enrich sparse preference data with additional information. The proposed algorithm is designed to enhance the efficiency of a user's local bi-cluster while maintaining robust performance across the entire dataset. Comprehensive evaluations using both real-world and synthetic data demonstrate that the method outperforms state-of-the-art algorithms in terms of accuracy, while also offering significant improvements in scalability and speed.

This study investigates how solar magnetic activity affects the spectral line shapes of the Sun by analyzing high-resolution, disk-integrated spectra from the HARPS-N spectrograph. We examine spectral line profiles across the 4300–6800 Å range, covering both magnetically sensitive lines and those that are generally considered immune to magnetic fields. To assess magnetic influence, we tracked the evolution of magnetically sensitive lines using two indicators: the Equivalent Width (EW) and the Balmer Excess (BH). Our analysis reveals that variations in magnetically sensitive lines are detectable throughout the solar cycle, with a specific correlation to BH variations occurring during descending phases of the cycle. We further explored the correlation between magnetically sensitive line changes and the Doppler shift of the G-band, a proxy for granulation changes, finding a correlation during the cycle's descent. Additionally, we evaluated magnetically sensitive line evolution against sunspot groups and plages, identifying a clear correlation with the total area of sunspot groups, particularly in the 4300–5300 Å range. Finally, we demonstrated that the EW and BH serve as effective proxies for estimating the magnetic flux of sunspot groups.

This study investigates tunneling spectroscopy of Majorana zero modes (MZMs) in tunneling setups where the normal-side electrode is connected to a resistance, causing the MMZ signal to diverge from spurious peaks caused by trivial Andreev bound states (ABSs). We demonstrate that at energies below the topological gap, resistance induces peak broadening that increases with energy, whereas ideal zero-width peaks remain unchanged. Consequently, resistively degraded full-gap ABSs can be distinguished from MZMs by normal conductance scaling: ABSs follow a linear increase in width with energy, while MZMs maintain constant width. We anticipate this approach will offer a practical solution for identifying true MZMs amidst background ABSs in future experiments.

Forward image tone mapping modifies the dynamic range of an input image according to a specific target look, whereas reverse tone mapers perform the inverse by recovering original dynamic ranges from high-contrast images. This study introduces a new framework for both processes that utilizes pairs consisting of a standard dynamic-range image and a high-contrast image to derive stylistic characteristics. The method first identifies a set of style descriptors from these pairs and subsequently employs Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) to adjust the tones of any given low-dynamic image so it aligns with the extracted style. This approach enables the separation of style from content and supports the creation of multiple variations from a single photo. The system was evaluated using both real and synthetic datasets, including one created through simulated tone mapping, and achieved superior performance compared to existing techniques based on quantitative metrics, visual quality, and user studies.

This study introduces the AQTC dataset, which is dedicated to identifying ambiguous questions within customer support ticket documents. The data comprises 1,048 instances drawn from GitHub repositories for various software projects, where each instance includes a source text segment, a query, and a corresponding answer. These examples were manually annotated to include an ambiguous question token and labels for the entity types present in the text. The authors propose a hybrid framework that combines large language models with rule-based systems to detect such queries. The framework leverages the pre-trained BERT model for semantic understanding and utilizes pattern matching to identify specific keywords and structural features. Experimental results indicate that this method outperforms baseline approaches, achieving an F1 score of 0.899.

Recent research has revealed that the accumulation of snow on the ground exhibits a self-affine character when observed across multiple spatial scales. This study offers a proof that the turbulence within the atmosphere preferentially selects spatial locations for snow deposition. The evidence supporting this preferential selection is found in the fact that the structure function exponent of the exponent is less than two—a result derived from the principle of preferential selection itself. Furthermore, the magnitude of this exponent's less-than-two value is determined by the ratio of two Kolmogorov-like exponents representing spatial velocity and snowflake fall speeds. Finally, the fractal dimension of snowflake clusters is linked to this same exponent less-than-two value through a universal relationship.

This paper introduces the application of active inference, a recent theory of brain function, to robot navigation within unknown environments. By utilizing only a high-level prior of an unknown world's structure, the system generates its own sensory prediction model through active learning while planning actions to achieve predefined goals. The robot acquires knowledge of the world by comparing predicted versus actual sensory inputs, employing a hierarchical architecture that allows a high-level policy to guide low-level motor behaviors. High-level policy selection is determined by maximizing expected reward, approximated via Monte Carlo simulations. Experimental results demonstrate that a physical robot using this hierarchical active inference framework can navigate unfamiliar spaces and create accurate world representations, all while requiring minimal unknown data.

High-precision, high-speed tracking of charged particle trajectories within multi-layered Time Projection Chambers (TPCs) is essential for contemporary particle physics experiments. However, transmitting the massive point cloud data generated by these detectors to tracking algorithms presents significant challenges due to limited inter-device communication bandwidth. To overcome this, we introduce a communication-efficient data compression framework that treats raw TPC sparse cloud data as effective sparse tensors, enabling compression through dual Convex Autoencoders (CAEs). We detail specific strategies for sparsifying the TPC point clouds to achieve Dual-TPC Sparse Tensor representation and employ a customized loss function that preserves the critical features of 3D sparse tensor data during reconstruction. Experimental outcomes demonstrate that this proposed method surpasses both the CAE-based approach using standard loss functions and the established lossless compression standard, Huffman coding.

The Finzi gravity model offers a novel framework of modified gravitational theory, characterized by three free parameters that can be constrained by observational data. In this study, we statistically characterize galaxy clusters within the Finzi framework by examining the redshift distribution, luminosity function, and halo mass function. The redshift analysis indicates a higher density of clusters at higher redshifts under Finzi gravity compared to the $\Lambda$CDM model, a trend that intensifies with higher mass thresholds. Conversely, the luminosity function exhibits a higher abundance of clusters at lower luminosities in the Finzi scenario relative to $\Lambda$CDM predictions. Additionally, the Finzi model forecasts a higher number of halos at lower mass limits and greater numbers at higher redshifts when contrasted with the $\Lambda$CDM model.

A $k$-uniform hypergraph is defined as a set of subsets, each containing $k$ vertices, drawn from a finite ground set $V$. Such a hypergraph is termed convex if, for every pair of vertices $u$ and $v$, the subsets forming the hypergraph are subsets of the complete $k$-uniform hypergraph on the path connecting $u$ and $v$ within the hypercube $\{0,1\}^{V}$. In this context, the path between two points consists of all minimal-dimensional binary vectors that are linear combinations with non-negative coefficients of the vectors $u$ and $v$. The paper investigates the saturation problem for these convex hypergraphs: given an arbitrary finite set $\mathcal{F}$ of examples, the task involves determining the maximum number of edges possible in a convex $k$-uniform hypergraph that excludes every configuration isomorphic to an element of $\mathcal{F}$. The authors establish that this maximum number of edges exhibits a saturation behavior, meaning it is bounded above by $O(n^{k-1+\epsilon})$ for any $\epsilon > 0$, with the upper bound's tightness demonstrated for specific cases of $\mathcal{F}$.

A comprehensive $\alpha$-particle generation mechanism for the photodisintegration of $^{6}$Li is established, utilizing an extensive dataset of the $^{51}$V($\gamma$,p)$^{51}$Ti and $^{51}$V($\gamma$,n)$^{51}$Cr reactions. This mechanism is implemented within the TALYS 1.9 framework to investigate the $\gamma$-$n$-$p$ reaction channels on lithium-6. The study reveals that the $\gamma$-$n$-$p$ cross-sections are sensitive to the incident $\gamma$-ray energy, the spin and parity of the excited states in $^{6}$Li, and the cross-sections for the $\gamma$-$p$-$n$ channel. Additionally, the influence of the $\gamma$-$p$-$n$ channel on the $\gamma$-$n$-$p$ process is examined, and the $\gamma$-$n$-$n$-$p$ reaction channels in $^{6}$Li are analyzed.

This study introduces a new eel-inspired climbing robot designed to ascend vertical surfaces, utilizing a novel locomotion strategy derived from research on Pacific eels (*Anactenes pacificus*). By integrating a bio-mimetic control framework, the robot replicates the specific undulatory movements observed in eels to achieve effective vertical ascent. Furthermore, the research presents a new actuation method that combines pneumatic and electric systems, offering an innovative approach to soft robotics. This hybrid power source drives both a multi-mode transition from a flat, wall-parallel posture to an ascending configuration and a unique tri-planar undulation pattern. Experimental results confirm the robot's stability and capability to climb across various actuation frequencies while maintaining a wall-parallax stance.

This paper introduces a novel, data-driven methodology for creating optimal, patient-specific therapies for colon cancer. The study utilizes a continuous-time Markov process to simulate the immune system's response to colon cancer, employing the Fokker-Planck equation to track the time-evolution of the probability density function regarding immune cell counts. An optimization framework is established to determine the best continuous or discontinuous continuous-time treatment strategy, aiming to minimize the long-term probability of cancer cell survival. The validity of the proposed model and its application to colon cancer are demonstrated through numerical experiments.

Deep Learning (D2D) has emerged as a vital component of next-generation wireless systems, offering significant advantages over conventional D2D scheduling techniques that rely on channel quality indicators (CQI) feedback and suffer from high computational complexity. To address this, we introduce an innovative D2D scheduling approach centered on Era of Information (IoI) principles, utilizing a deep learning methodology to optimize energy efficiency within small-scale scenarios. Specifically, we propose a Deep Q-Network (DQN) framework that enables user equipment (UE) to autonomously select scheduling moments and transmit data directly without the need for CQI reporting to the base station. Furthermore, we derive a closed-form expression for energy efficiency and employ it to analytically determine the optimal parameters for the DQN. Numerical evaluations demonstrate that this learning-based solution outperforms traditional methods in terms of both energy efficiency and computational complexity.
